title: Designing the Optimal Snowboard Half-Pipe

source.pdf_page_offset_note: PDF pages and printed page numbers coincide; page 1 is the title and opening summary page.

context_sources.use: Official contest summary of Problem A: maximize vertical air, tailor the shape for other requirements such as twist, and determine practical-course tradeoffs.
Official designation of control 11199 as Outstanding Winner with INFORMS and Ben Fusaro awards.

limitations: All 21 pages were rendered at 144 DPI and visually reviewed; formula-, table-, and figure-critical pages 5-18 received full-resolution checks.
Extracted mathematical glyphs are incomplete in places, so central equations were read from rendered pages.
No code, solver recurrence, numeric cutoff, input file, or machine-readable figure data accompany the paper.
Official context pages 1-2 establish the task and award provenance but provide no causal judge commentary.

required_outputs: Determine a half-pipe cross-section that maximizes vertical air, defined as maximum vertical distance above the coping.
Tailor the shape for another performance requirement such as maximum twist or rotation.
Determine the tradeoffs required to develop a practical course.
paper_interpretation: Treat frictionless vertical air as shape-independent at fixed entry energy and equal coping height.
Use minimum traversal time as a spectator-oriented secondary objective and derive a cycloid.
Add Coulomb loss and compare semicircle, cycloid, and flat-oval families by simulated exit speed.
Reduce rotation to airtime divided by a fixed rotation period and discuss pumping qualitatively.
Conclude that vertical air and rotation prefer opposing geometric extremes.
task_reconstruction.coverage_note: The paper addresses both named performance branches and states a tradeoff, but it does not produce a constrained, buildable compromise for the official practical-course requirement.

section_map.summary: Introduces optimal half-pipe design and the two performance branches.
Motivates vertical air and average rotation using judged-performance context.
Defines course components and summarizes historical Olympic dimensions.
Lists seven common physical and geometric assumptions.
Uses energy conservation and introduces the brachistochrone objective.
Applies calculus of variations and gives a geometric cycloid construction.
Defines tangent, normal, curvature, force balance, and energy loss.
Parameterizes semicircle and cycloid candidates by arc length.
Defines flat ovals and fixes width, entry speed, and friction for comparison.
Presents aligned speed trajectories and candidate result tables.
Compares curve families across width and reports numerical discretization.
States a limiting flat-oval optimum and discusses drag, friction, slope, and surfaces.
Relates horizontal takeoff, deeper landing, airtime, and rotation.
Describes a qualitative tradeoff between vertical air and rotation.
Lists engineering, physics, sports-performance, and general sources.

contributions.summary: Separates shape-independent frictionless exit energy from traversal-time entertainment value.
Derives and geometrically explains the cycloid as a brachistochrone baseline.
Builds a mass-independent speed-squared equation that exposes width and curvature contributions to Coulomb loss.
Defines three interpretable curve families and compares them under multiple controlled quantities.
Pairs trajectory plots with compact candidate tables and short interpretations.
Enumerates multiple omitted physical mechanisms and possible extensions.
Makes the vertical-air versus rotation conflict explicit instead of asserting one universal design.

nodes.label: Flat oval ranks highest among tested families
Ballistic airtime and fixed rotation period
Deep, wide walls claimed to favor rotation

critical_dependency_failures: M2 silently changes the nonzero entry-speed baseline and does not close arbitrary fixed height and width under smooth symmetry.
M4 compares geometries with different depths and reaches a zero-height, infinite-curvature boundary rather than a practical optimum.
M3 conflates snow friction and aerodynamic drag and permits negative kinetic energy without a stopping event.
M5 uses an incorrect launch-angle equation and a fixed rotation period despite posture-dependent inertia.
M6 contains no takeoff impulse, trajectory, angular momentum, or landing equations.
D1 has no constrained Pareto or stakeholder decision model.

assumptions.summary: Requires a left-right symmetric cross-section for stance fairness and repeated jumps.
Treats rider and board as rigid and inelastic and applies ideal dry-friction reasoning.
Removes body orientation, board flex, active pumping, and distributed contact.
Uses one constant Coulomb coefficient for the entire path.
Requires continuity, inward concavity, and near-vertical coping tangents.
Reduces the problem to a flat two-dimensional cross-section.
Sets unit mass, entry speed 20 m/s, width 18 m, and mu 0.05 for the main comparison.
Assumes equal athlete skill, fixed rotation period, negligible airborne drag, and initially vertical flight.
Assumes horizontal takeoff produces a deeper landing and longer airtime without solving the trajectory.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Cites total airtime and average degree of rotation as variables correlated with judged score.
Tabulates approximate length, gradient, width, and wall height for four Olympic courses.
Uses a grooming-machine diagram and recommended dimensions to motivate modern super-pipes.
Uses a cited broad coefficient range and selects mu 0.05 without condition-specific calibration.
Uses 0.01 m path steps and mentions an unspecified smaller-step rerun.
Selects final-jump images, trick descriptions, scores, and standings for two Vancouver athletes without a tracking protocol.

models.summary: Conservation of energy makes frictionless exit energy shape-independent at equal coping height.
Minimizes time from coping to midpoint using the classical brachistochrone functional.
Uses a Beltrami/Euler-Lagrange first integral to derive a cycloid, with a typo in the displayed y equation.
Relates normal force to gravity and curvature-dependent centripetal load, but the theta convention is inconsistent.
Expresses exit speed squared as entry speed squared minus width loss and curvature-weighted loss.
Parameterizes a semicircle by arc length and constant curvature.
Uses cycloid y, curvature, width, and length formulas but prints an invalid x(s) and unspecified truncation.
Defines a flat oval as a horizontal segment with two quarter circles.
Uses ballistic airtime T=2v0/g and R=T/t under a fixed rotation period.
Describes pumping, horizontal velocity, deeper landing, and added airtime only qualitatively.

verification.summary: Checks that exit speed is independent of rider mass under the chosen force law.
Explains the zero-curvature width-loss case as a limiting check.
Repeats candidate comparison at fixed total arc length, but other geometry dimensions still change.
Acknowledges discretization error and an unspecified smaller-step rerun without quantitative convergence.
Sweeps mu but fails to treat zero and negative energy as stopping or infeasible events.
Attempts an angle-sensitivity calculation, but the formula fails its zero-angle limit and understates the effect.
Uses a two-athlete landing comparison as causal evidence despite severe confounding.
Provides no measured trajectory, speed, airtime, load, rotation, or landing validation.

results_trace.summary: Reports shape independence under fixed entry energy and equal coping height.
Names the cycloid as the frictionless entertainment-time optimum.
Reports exit speeds 15.7, 14.0, 16.5, and 16.0 m/s for the four candidate cases.
Reports exit speeds 15.7, 12.6, 16.1, and 15.8 m/s with different resulting widths.
Ranks the long flat oval above the other tested families across the plotted widths.
Extrapolates to a straight line with infinitesimal quarter circles, a degenerate and infeasible boundary.
Claims less than 0.3 percent height change at 20 degrees; correct projectile geometry gives about 11.7 percent loss.
Makes maximum rotation equivalent to maximum airtime under fixed rotation period.
Leaves the practical answer as a qualitative preference between opposing geometric extremes.

writing_logic.summary: Moves from judged performance to two measurable design objectives.
Front-loads a numbered assumption list before derivation.
Starts with conservation, then changes the objective to traversal time, then adds friction.
Defines each candidate family before showing comparable plots and tables.
Changes fixed variables across experiments to investigate width, length, and curvature effects.
Names omitted mechanisms and possible extensions before the rotation branch.
Returns to the two objectives but does not close the official practical-course decision quantitatively.

language_observations.summary: Defines vertical air and rotation variables early, supporting a general technical audience.
Clearly signals that minimum travel time is an entertainment objective rather than vertical air itself.
Explains the physical meaning of width and curvature terms after displaying the model.
Candidly acknowledges visible discretization error but uses confidence language stronger than the reported test.
Says omitting slope causes no loss of generality without a coupled derivation or bound.
Uses causal wording for a two-athlete illustrative comparison.
Avoids a false universal optimum but stops short of an actionable conditional recommendation.

visualization_observations.summary: Course components, historical dimensions, and grooming geometry provide a concrete engineering baseline.
Three candidate profiles make fixed-height and fixed-width path choices visually intuitive.
A rolling-circle construction complements the variational derivation of the cycloid.
The force diagram is central but its angle and component labels conflict with the equations.
Aligned trajectories and a result table create a strong model-to-output visual rhythm.
A second comparison changes the controlled quantity and reports resulting widths.
Caption says speed while the vertical axis is kinetic energy, and candidate constraints remain unmatched.
Friction sensitivity is visible, but infeasible zero and negative energy states are unlabeled.
Landing stills explain the pumping story but do not provide controlled empirical validation.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: Official results confirm Outstanding, INFORMS, and Ben Fusaro designations but provide no causal judge commentary.
The calculus-of-variations derivation, geometric construction, and curvature-dependent energy model may have made the solution feel mathematically distinctive.
Repeated candidate plots, tables, and short interpretations may have helped judges compare alternatives quickly.

The two-objective architecture, broad limitation discussion, and explicit no-universal-optimum conclusion may have outweighed technical defects, but award status cannot establish this causal explanation.

weaknesses.summary: Dry-friction area independence is incorrectly extended to aerodynamic shape independence.
The paper says point-mass reduction only removes rotational energy, omitting several coupled mechanisms.
The brachistochrone derivation silently changes from fixed entry kinetic energy to zero entry speed.
A full smooth symmetric cycloid cannot satisfy arbitrary fixed height and width.
The displayed y parameter is r(theta-cos theta) instead of r(1-cos theta).
Theta is declared relative to horizontal while formulas require the complementary angle.
The printed cycloid x(s) has wrong units and fails a tangent-norm check.
An unspecified cusp cutoff is not propagated to width, length, or endpoint angle.
Candidate families change depth and other dimensions while being interpreted as shape effects.
One uncalibrated mu combines snow and air losses.
A width-18 m semicircle is incorrectly called radius 18 m while using radius-9 m arc length.
Figure 14 caption and vertical axis disagree between speed and kinetic energy.
The smaller-step check has no step, error, values, or convergence rate.
The preferred path approaches zero height and infinite curvature.
Curvature-dependent Coulomb loss is incorrectly treated as quadratic aerodynamic drag.
Figure 17 includes negative kinetic energy without stopping or infeasibility handling.
The claim of no loss of generality for a two-dimensional cross-section is unsupported.
The angle correction fails at zero deviation and understates 20-degree height loss by roughly two orders of magnitude.
Internal posture changes and time-varying inertia are wrongly excluded from airborne rotation.
The central pumping mechanism has no dynamic equations.
Two different athletes and tricks cannot establish that deeper landing causes more rotation or score.
No feasible multi-objective compromise, uncertainty analysis, or construction decision is produced.
Code, recurrence, cutoff, data, and implementation details are missing.

independent_extensions.title: Feasible curve optimization
independent_extensions.procedure: Optimize splines or clothoids at common width and depth with tangent, curvature, curvature-rate, normal-load, contact, construction, and safety constraints.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Removes the zero-height and infinite-curvature degeneracy.

independent_extensions.title: Separated dissipation
independent_extensions.procedure: Calibrate snow Coulomb friction, aerodynamic drag, plowing or deformation, and active rider work as distinct terms with stopping and contact events.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Restores physical units, geometry dependence, and testable parameters.

independent_extensions.title: Analytic ODE checks
independent_extensions.procedure: Differentiate the energy integral, solve the linear psi ODE by integrating factor, and use exact piecewise-circle cases to test the numerical solver.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Provides independent solution and convergence benchmarks.

independent_extensions.title: Aerial multibody model
independent_extensions.procedure: Couple takeoff impulse, projectile motion, conserved angular momentum, time-varying inertia, opening time, wall intersection, and landing load.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Turns airtime into a feasible rotation and landing prediction.

independent_extensions.title: Tracked-run validation
independent_extensions.procedure: Use repeated multi-athlete video or inertial tracking to validate speed, takeoff angle, airtime, rotation, landing point, and load under known geometry and snow conditions.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Separates mechanism validity from qualitative plausibility.

independent_extensions.title: Practical Pareto design
independent_extensions.procedure: Report Pareto alternatives over vertical rise, rotation feasibility, peak load, fall risk, footprint, snow volume, construction tolerance, and uncertainty.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Answers the official practical-course tradeoff requirement conditionally and transparently.

candidate_rule_impacts.summary: Creates a matched-geometry, nondegenerate, feasible physical-path optimization workflow.
Separates surface, air, deformation, and active-work losses and enforces physical events.
Creates a takeoff-flight-posture-landing model for twist and aerial rotation.
Creates a fair candidate-design visualization and decision-comparison contract.

unresolved_questions: What exact numerical recurrence, cusp cutoff, and smaller step were used?
Did the implementation use the printed invalid cycloid x(s), or only the correct y(s), curvature, width, and length?
Which snow, board, temperature, speed, posture, and air conditions support the cited friction range?
How would matched height and width plus human-load constraints change the candidate ranking?
What features did INFORMS or Ben Fusaro judges cite? No reviewed official commentary answers this.
